title: Relay Yard
summary: An MCP server that lets an AI client inspect a production database safely: every question becomes a reviewed, read-only query with a row budget and an audit trail, so an assistant can answer “why is this slow” without being trusted to change anything.
role: Solo — schema introspection, the query guard, the MCP surface and the audit log.
context:
Every team has the same debugging loop: a slow endpoint, a screenshot of a dashboard, and a database nobody is allowed to query from a laptop. The person who can answer the question is busy; the person asking cannot reach the data.

Handing a database to a language model sounds like the obvious shortcut, and it is also how an assistant finds a table, invents a join, and returns a confident number from the wrong column. The real problem is not access. It is making access narrow enough that a wrong answer is visible.

solution.title: Schema map before any question
solution.body: The server reads the catalog once — tables, columns, types, foreign keys, indexes — and gives the model that map instead of the data. The model can name a column only if the column exists, which removes the most common hallucination before it is written.

solution.title: A guarded query path
solution.body: Generated SQL is parsed and accepted only when it is a single read-only statement against an allowlisted schema. Writes, DDL and cross-database reads are rejected, and the rejection explains which rule failed.

solution.title: Row budget and timeout
solution.body: Every query runs inside a transaction with a statement timeout and a row cap. A missing filter returns a truncated sample plus a warning, not a million rows into a chat window.

solution.title: Audit trail
solution.body: Each call records the question, the accepted SQL, the duration and the row count. The answer can always be traced back to the exact query that produced it, which is what makes the result reviewable by someone else.

contribution: Solo project. I wrote the catalog introspection, the SQL guard, the MCP tool surface and the audit log, and I use it on my own projects. It runs against a read replica with a role that cannot write, so the guard is a second line of defence rather than the only one.
approach:
The first version gave the model a text-to-SQL tool and reviewed the output by reading it. That failed for a predictable reason: reviewing SQL is the same skill as writing it, so the review added latency without adding certainty.

The second version moved the review into code. The model proposes; a parser and an allowlist decide. The simpler option — one prompt that asks the model to be careful — was rejected because a prompt is not a boundary.
aiRole: The model translates a question into a query and explains the result. It never holds a database credential, never writes, and never sees more rows than the budget allows. It can also be wrong about which table answers the question, so the reply always includes the SQL and the row count; a person confirms the interpretation, and the audit log keeps the evidence.
quote: A prompt is not a permission boundary.

technicalDecisions.title: Give the model the schema, not the rows
technicalDecisions.body: Catalog metadata is small, stable and safe to send. Sample rows are neither. Describing columns, types and relationships keeps the model accurate about names without exposing customer data, and it makes the first turn predictable in cost.

technicalDecisions.title: Parse the SQL instead of trusting the prompt
technicalDecisions.body: An allowlist over a parsed statement survives a model that ignores instructions. It also produces a specific error — “write statements are not allowed here” — which the model can act on, so the failure teaches the next attempt.

technicalDecisions.title: Read replica as the outer boundary
technicalDecisions.body: The guard is code and code has bugs; a role without write grants does not. Two independent boundaries cost one connection string and remove the worst possible outcome.

outcomes: A question about a slow table is answered in one exchange, with the query and the row count attached.
Incorrect table choices surface as an obviously wrong result instead of a plausible sentence, because the SQL is always part of the answer.
The guard has rejected every write attempt, including the ones phrased as a “quick fix”.
Running it against my own schema shortened the loop between reading a migration and understanding its effect.
confidentialityNote: Sample entry — the product is fictional and no database or client is described. A real version would name the environment it reads and what the audit log retains.
